data.title: Data center sparks battle on London’s Brick Lane
data.description:
While data centers need space if Britain is serious about AI sovereignty, environmental advocates say that city planners have used the issue as ‘a kind of Trojan horse for bad development’

In Brick Lane, the historic heart of London’s Bangladeshi community, residents oppose plans for a data center in a disused brewery, citing the erosion of heritage and need for social housing.

“This has really been the focal point of the British Bangladeshi community,” local councilor Faysal Ahmed told reporters, recalling a time when his parents ran a restaurant beneath his childhood home in the lane.

While many curry houses remain, the street and the surrounding neighborhood is transforming, in part to help power the British capital’s digital infrastructure boom.

Part of a multimillion-pound redevelopment of the sprawling former Truman brewery site, the East End financial data center is an unlikely addition to the graffiti-lined Brick Lane, where tourists spill between vintage shops and line up for bagels served through the night.

The 7.5 hectare site would also be transformed by new offices and retail space, primarily serving the neighboring financial district filled with skyscrapers.

Approval of the development by the British government comes as a boom in water and energy-hungry data centers — particularly as demand rises for facilities supporting artificial intelligence — fuels local opposition worldwide.

For Ahmed, the development uses land that could help house some of the roughly 31,000 residents on the waiting list for social housing in the Tower Hamlets district.

The redevelopment plans are for only 44 apartments, including just six for social housing, prompting residents to recently protest outside the British Ministry of Housing.

“My personal concern is about the need for affordable social housing for young people and preserving the heritage, the special character, of the area,” said Susanna Kow, a member of the Save Brick Lane campaign.

According to planning documents, the Labour government gave “significant weight” to the benefits of additional data center capacity, citing the need to “meet the escalating demand driving emerging technologies such as [artificial intelligence] AI and increased digital services.”

The government’s housing department declined to comment on its decision in last month to approve the plans, while the Truman Brewery has not responded to a request for its reaction.

“We’ve been campaigning on planning issues and ... the incursion of the city on the East End for quite a number of years,” said Jonathan Moberly, who is leading local opposition.

Moberly said that the project was part of a “growing national issue about the amount of power taken from the grid that can stop other developments happening, like housing.”

The International Energy Agency in April reported that the global electricity demand of data centers grew by 17 percent last year.

It projects electricity consumption from centers will double over five years to 2030.

“The UK already faces a projected daily water deficit of nearly 5 billion liters by 2050,” according to a report on the UK government Web site. “National water resource plans ... do not adequately account for the burgeoning demand from infrastructure such as AI data centers. This oversight risks intensifying water stress in already vulnerable regions.”

For industry consultant Mark Acton, the infrastructure is increasingly essential, particularly in London, a city where proximity can provide the ultra-fast response times needed for financial trading.

“Everything we currently do digitally comes from a data center,” said Acton, who argued the facilities have become an easy target owing to what he said was a lack of understanding of their actual water and energy use.

If Britain is serious about sovereignty over its AI infrastructure, “you’ve got to have somewhere to put it,” Acton said.

However, campaigners at environmental charity Global Action Plan argue that UK planning rules have not kept pace with the expansion of the sector or adequately accounted for environmental costs.

“It’s been a kind of Trojan horse for bad development,” said Owen Espley, the group’s community campaigns manager. “We need local knowledge and input to go into shaping developments to improve them and make sure that we get better data centers at the end of it.”

Further down Brick Lane, Carol Burns, born and raised in the area, has no intention of going anywhere. Sitting inside the shop her family has run since the 1800s — its walls covered with family photographs — Burns is proud to be part of London’s East End community.

“People are always trying to buy this place, but no. They’ll have to drag me out of here feet-first,” she said in her thick Cockney accent.

data.title: Malawi’s mining offers promises and challenges
data.description:
A new generation of mining projects targeting rare earth and critical minerals could transform Malawi’s economy — but experts warn of the Africa-wide challenges in turning resource wealth into broad-based prosperity.

One of the world’s poorest countries, Malawi has long depended on agriculture, aid and a handful of exports such as tobacco, tea and sugar.

Now discoveries of rare earths and critical minerals potentially worth tens of billions of dollars are drawing the small southern African nation into the global scramble for materials essential for the energy transition and advanced manufacturing.

Critics warn that without stronger institutions, local participation and domestic processing, Malawi could repeat a pattern familiar in Africa of exporting valuable resources while reaping few benefits at home.

“This means a lot to us and expectations are very high,” said Malawian Member of Parliament Lawrence Chakakala Chaziya, whose constituency includes central Kasiya where Sovereign Metals, an Australian company, is advancing a major critical minerals project.

Sovereign Metals says the operation sits atop the world’s largest natural deposit of rutile — used in titanium production — and one of the largest of graphite, an important component of lithium-ion batteries.

“Given the large quantities of deposits here, we expect the mining project to bring tangible benefits to our people, particularly in terms of improved social services,” Chaziya said. “I have already urged our people not to sell their land.”

In the south, another Australian company is developing a project to extract rare earths used in powerful magnets for electric vehicles, wind turbines and other advanced technologies. Canadian and Australian groups are also developing other rare earths projects and reviving a long-dormant uranium mine.

Mining contributes about 1 percent of Malawi’s GDP, according to figures cited by the Malawian Chamber of Mines and Energy.

The World Bank estimates the sector could account for about 12 percent of GDP by next year. Cumulative mineral exports could reach US$30 billion from this year to 2040, with annual revenues approaching US$3 billion by 2034.

“Mining offers Malawi a realistic chance to diversify the economy, earn foreign exchange, create skilled jobs and build industries beyond agriculture,” said Gowokani Chijere-Chirwa, an economist at the University of Malawi.

The Malawian government has already moved to improve its hand by passing a law in 2023 removing a 10 percent ceiling on state participation in the sector.

It also plans a state mining company to pursue exploration, joint ventures and mineral beneficiation or upgrading of raw ores, Malawian Mining and Minerals Regulatory Authority Director-General Mphatso Chikoti said.

The country needs to produce skilled professionals, from geologists to lawyers with mining expertise, said Ahmed Dassu, a mining expert.

It should also shore up its geological mapping to “negotiate from a stronger position, attract credible investors and avoid giving away valuable resources without fully understanding their potential,” Dassu told reporters.

Like many resource-rich African countries, Malawi faces the challenge of breaking free from a colonial-era model that treats the continent as “a project of extractivism,” said Deprose Muchena from the Open Society Foundations, which supports African governments in policy development.

Muchena cited examples of major chromium producer Zimbabwe exporting virtually all its output, while the Democratic Republic of the Congo provides about 70 percent of the world’s cobalt, but processes only a fraction domestically.

Africa holds about 30 percent of the world’s critical mineral reserves, including cobalt, copper, lithium, nickel and rare earths, according to the UN, making it a focus of competition between the US and China for strategic resources.

Weak tax regimes and corruption further erode potential gains, with Africa losing about US$88 billion annually to illicit outflows such as underpricing exports or overpricing imports, Muchena said.

Mining projects should not be operating as a separate international enclave, but brought into economies to spur industrialization, he told reporters.

“Malawi has a very small window to turn around the discovery of minerals, of rare earths, into an opportunity for economic development,” he said.

data.title: Senegal eyes homemade satellites amid African space race
data.description:
Senegalese engineers in hairnets and white gloves are carefully assembling a nanosatellite at a French lab — another step toward fostering their own space industry at home.

Preparations are already under way for the building of satellites at a new headquarters for Sensat, Senegal’s national space program, outside Dakar — part of a breakneck push by several African space agencies jostling for their own piece of the final frontier.

“We have mastered the manufacturing process,” Gayane Faye, chief of Sensat, told reporters in the sterile lab at the University of Montpellier in southern France.

The engineers from Sensat built their first satellite — Gaindesat-1A — in collaboration with the Montpellier scientists, launching it in 2024. Gainde means “lion” in the local Wolof language.

NO MORE COACHING

For the follow-up, Gaindesat-1B, which is designed to collect environmental and climate data, “we’ve removed the coaching component,” Faye said.

It is part of a drive for technological independence by Senegal, mirrored in many parts of Africa.

Representatives from the continent were a key presence at the International Space Summit in Paris on Wednesday and Thursday.

Across Africa, national space budgets have grown to US$800 million, said Temidayo Oniosun, founder of Lagos-based consultancy Space in Africa, up from less than US$300 million in 2018.

That is a tiny fraction of the world total, which was US$132 billion in 2024, 60 percent of it from the US, but it is growing. The African Union has a new continental space agency in Cairo and the number of countries on the continent with a space program has jumped from eight to more than 20 since 2018, according to Oniosun.

Africa’s entry into space is not entirely new: Egypt launched its Nilesat 101 from French Guyana in 1998, a first for the continent.

Nigeria’s national space agency was founded the following year, sent its first device space-bound in 2003 and runs two satellites in orbit — one for communications and the other run by the military’s separate space agency, Oniosun said.

SOUTH AFRICA

South Africa, another historic player, is home to a ground station that has overseen communications for hundreds of launches and a second facility being developed with NASA is due to open within two years.

Italy built a satellite-launching station on the Kenyan coast in the 1960s that operated until 1988.

Kenya developed its own satellite, Taifa-1, that launched from a SpaceX rocket in 2023.

Even restive Somalia could have its own space port as part of a US$6 billion partnership with Turkey announced last year.

New players continue to join the rush: Ivory Coast named its first space agency director last month and is to host the African Space Expo later this month.

Better satellite data are seen as key for urban planning and environmental monitoring, which are major issues on a continent whose cities are growing at a rapid rate.

“For the first phase of Africa’s space development, success was often measured by whether a country could launch a satellite,” said Richard Folly of Togo-based African Geospace, whose company has worked on flood risk and disaster management. “The next phase has to ask a harder question: What economic, strategic or societal value is that satellite producing?”

There is also the question of independence in an industry still dominated by non-African space agencies and firms.

Despite the country’s long-running satellite program, Nigerian agencies “don’t build technology locally,” Oniosun said.

Senegal is determined to start generating its own satellite images, as “certain services cannot even be carried out because we lack the means to buy them,” Faye said.

For the next satellite, Sensat’s third, “we aim to move toward developing our own technology — specifically, our own payload to be flown on the satellite.” Then, if the infrastructure is ready, “the fourth satellite can be built entirely in Senegal.”

data.title: Micron to give engineers NT$1m, equity
data.description:
EQUAL SHARE: A row over Micron’s payouts coincides with a global debate about who deserves a cut of the sudden wealth generated by the artificial intelligence boom

Micron Technology Inc is to provide its engineers in Taiwan a cash bonus of NT$1 million (US$31,600) plus equity rewards, as the company’s local unions are demanding an additional payout to reflect their contribution to the chipmaker’s blowout profits.

The Idaho-based chipmaker said in a statement yesterday that its entry-level, Taiwan-based engineers’ average compensation would reach NT$3.4 million for the past fiscal year after the cash and equities awards. All employees in Taiwan would receive equities as part of the annual merit grants, the company added.

Before the announcement, Micron’s unions asked for a one-time cash payout equal to about seven years of an employee’s base salary. That would translate into an average payment of about US$170,000 per worker, based on Bloomberg calculations off data the unions provided. They are also demanding the company allocate a portion of its profit to be shared with global employees as bonuses going forward.

The row over Micron’s payouts coincides with a global debate about who deserves a cut of the sudden wealth generated by booming investment in artificial intelligence (AI)-related data centers and other infrastructure.

That has spurred Micron’s South Korean rivals Samsung Electronics Co and SK Hynix Inc to promise employees a share of the profits in their bonuses. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co has also vowed to set aside 30 percent more in profit-sharing payouts for employees.

However, the size of some of the bonuses has created rifts within companies and communities, with growing calls that users who supply AI with the data it needs also get a cut.

Micron has been handed a major boost from the AI boom. Its cutting-edge high-bandwidth memory is required to make AI accelerators from the likes of Nvidia Corp. The US chipmaker reported a 15-fold gain in net income in the third quarter, while its share price has risen more than 500 percent over the past year.

Micron employs about 15,000 people in Taiwan, which serves as a key manufacturing hub for the chipmaker.

At the same time, it still relies on the US for the bulk of its research and development operations and some production, while it also runs plants in Japan and Singapore.

The US memory maker and the Taoyuan union failed to reach an agreement during a mediation meeting last week, with a second round of mediation scheduled.

Micron is looking to avoid being dragged into a crisis similar to what Samsung Electronics faced in May, when a planned 18-day strike was called off after last-minute negotiations and a successful deal that created a special bonus pool worth 10.5 percent of the chip division’s operating profit, subject to profitability targets.

Additional reporting by Reuters

data.title: INTERVIEW: AI pushes banks beyond traditional processing
data.description:
BEYOND TRADITION: The rise of digital assets is reshaping custodians from passive asset holders into trusted providers of digital market infrastructure, Standard Chartered said

Artificial intelligence (AI), real-time payments and digital assets are pushing corporate treasury management beyond traditional transaction processing, giving companies faster visibility over cash and liquidity while enabling more automated and programmable payments, Standard Chartered Bank said.

The shift is creating new opportunities for Taiwan as it builds a regulatory framework for digital assets, with clearer rules for tokenized securities and stablecoins needed to support the development of the market, according to Standard Chartered Financing and Securities Services regional head Pierre Mengal.

“The rise of digital assets and tokenized securities is reshaping traditional custodians from passive asset holders into trusted providers of digital market infrastructure,” Mengal said during an one-on-one interview on Wednesday after attending the bank’s treasury forum in Taipei.

Standard Chartered identified six trends shaping the future of corporate treasury: real-time treasury management, programmable liquidity, the use of AI in treasury operations, and the growing commercial use of tokenization and digital assets.

These technologies are allowing companies to extract more value from payment data while making resilience a competitive advantage, the bank said.

Digital assets are gradually moving from an emerging financial technology toward practical applications in payments, custody and treasury management, Mengal said.

Their integration with real-time payments and new financial infrastructure could further accelerate the move toward more automated and connected financial operations, he said.

Taiwan took a step toward developing its digital-asset market in June when the legislature passed the Virtual Asset Services Act (虛擬資產服務法), establishing a legal framework covering virtual-asset service providers, custody, cybersecurity, asset segregation and internal controls.

The next priority should be regulatory clarity for tokenized securities and stablecoins, including rules governing ownership, custody, settlement, taxation and accounting, Mengal said.

Taiwan’s established capital-market infrastructure could provide a strong foundation for banks, custodians and securities firms to support the issuance, custody and settlement of tokenized assets, he said.

The market could also explore the use of stablecoins and tokenized deposits for cross-border payments, securities settlement and corporate treasury management, Mengal said.

“Digital financial transformation is redefining the growth path of companies, allowing them to gain more flexible ways to manage cross-border funds,” he said.

Such tools could help Taiwanese companies expanding overseas manage cross-border funds more efficiently while strengthening operational resilience, he said.

The growing use of AI, real-time data and digital assets is also changing how companies view resilience. Rather than being limited to risk management, resilience is increasingly becoming a strategic advantage as businesses seek to respond more quickly to changes in liquidity, payments and operating conditions, he said.

Standard Chartered has expanded its digital-asset capabilities in the past few years, covering custody, trading, tokenization and stablecoins, he said.

data.title: Enterprise AI use to fuel demand for cloud services
data.description:
Cloud service management company eCloudvalley Digital Technology Co (伊雲谷) yesterday said that it expected the growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) agents among enterprises to fuel demand for cloud services, systems integration and long-term subscriptions as early adopters are entering the full deployment stage from proof-of-concept trials.

ECloudvalley, which integrates and deploys public cloud services from Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Corp’s Azure and Alphabet Inc’s Google Cloud for enterprise customers, unveiled its first extensive enterprise AI portfolio yesterday.

The portfolio integrates services from eCloudvalley’s subsidiaries — CloudRiches Digital Technology Co (雲馥數位), Dynacloud Co (雲動力資訊), NeuroBrain Dynamics Inc (創智動能) and eCloudEdge Digital Innovation Co (雲界數位創新) — to support large-scale AI deployment.

The company aims to address tool fragmentation, data silos, cybersecurity, cost and governance challenges as the use of AI agents expands, it said.

It also aims to help companies scale AI from individual proof-of-concept trials to cross-department deployment, the company said.

“As the use of AI agents expands, enterprises’ cloud consumption will also grow,” eCloudvalley founder and chairman MP Tsai (蔡佳宏) said.

Major cloud service providers are offering incentives to capture this growing demand by encouraging customers to use AI models available on their platforms, Tsai said.

As it is time-consuming and costly to build private on-premises cloud infrastructure, new enterprise cloud service adopters usually turn to public cloud services to gain quick access to AI models, he said.

As a result, eCloudvalley is gaining new customers, while existing customers are also increasing their cloud consumption as they expand AI applications, he added.

The trend is also driving recurring demand for cloud consumption, platform subscriptions, AI governance and maintenance services, Tsai said.

ECloudvalley’s customer renewal rate is about 96 percent, while one-off projects account for only a small portion of its business, he said.

Since last year, eCloudvalley has seen more enterprises adopt AI agents, eCloudvalley AI business unit head Christine Wang (王玟樺) said.

“Nearly all customers that conducted AI agent POC trials with the company over the past two to three years have moved into production environments,” she said.

Some enterprises have also expanded from adopting a single AI agent to second and third agents integrating into daily operations, she added.

Most early adopters expand AI applications to other departments, including customer service, finance, maintenance and manufacturing, after completing their first projects, Wang said.

Enterprises therefore need to track how many AI agents they have, who developed them, the models and data they use, their access permissions, costs and effectiveness, she said.

To address this, eCloudvalley introduced the Multi-AI Agent Hub and ECV AI Governance platform to integrate agents across platforms and departments, while centrally managing models, data, access rights, costs and execution records, Wang said.

Looking ahead, enterprises need AI agents to operate continuously and reliably, making the usage limits common in individual subscription services unsuitable, Tsai said.

eCloudvalley plans to discuss new collaboration models with enterprise customers, Anthropic PBC and OpenAI, leveraging its systems-integration capabilities and forward-deployed engineering team, he said.

data.title: Tax revenue surges amid boom in stock market
data.description:
Tax revenue surged last month as a stock market boom drove a sharp increase in securities transaction taxes, helping push government tax collections to a record pace in the first eight months of the year.

Tax revenue rose 28.9 percent from a year earlier to NT$198.2 billion (US$6.26 billion) last month, the Ministry of Finance said yesterday. Securities transaction tax revenue jumped 94.5 percent to NT$54 billion, its 13th consecutive month of annual growth.

The increase reflects the growing contribution of Taiwan’s buoyant stock market to government coffers, as demand for artificial intelligence (AI)-related stocks has lifted trading activity and generated more tax revenue.

Liu Shun-rong (劉訓蓉), Department of Statistics Deputy Director, said the increase was driven by a sharp rise in stock trading activity.

Average daily stock-market turnover reached NT$1.09 trillion last month, nearly doubling from a year earlier, as domestic and overseas investors increased their exposure to local shares benefiting from the AI boom, Liu said.

For the first eight months, average daily turnover climbed 1.7-fold from a year earlier, providing a major boost to securities transaction tax revenue and helping strengthen government finances.

Housing-related tax revenue also improved last month. Property-related income tax revenue rose 33.2 percent from a year earlier, while land value increment tax increased 22.7 percent and deed tax gained 15.3 percent.

Liu said the gains reflected a broad improvement in housing-related tax collections.

However, for the first eight months property-related income tax revenue was still down 1.1 percent from a year earlier, although the decline narrowed significantly.

Not all tax categories benefited from broader economic recovery.

Commodity tax revenue fell 20.2 percent in the first eight months to NT$77.4 billion, Liu said. The decline was mainly due to tax cuts on gasoline and diesel, lower tax collections on imported vehicles and increased tax refunds for newly purchased vehicles.

Total tax revenue for the first eight months reached NT$3.75 trillion, up 25.2 percent from a year earlier. The sharp increase underscores how the stock-market rally, fueled in part by Taiwan’s central role in the global AI supply chain, has become an increasingly important source of government revenue.

data.title: DeepSeek tests South Korean memory makers’ stocks with demand doubts
data.description:
Fund managers wading back into South Korean memory makers’ stocks got a fresh gut check after DeepSeek’s latest artificial intelligence (AI) model raised doubts on the strength of demand.

SK Hynix Inc and Samsung Electronics Co shares dipped 2.2 and 3.5 percent respectively yesterday, paring their nascent rebound from July’s steep selloff. DeepSeek’s comment that it has reduced the amount of high-bandwidth memory required in its AI models added to concerns on tech amid fears of US interest rate hikes.

Sentiment toward the chip duo had been improving on signs of continued Big Tech spending, along with cheap stock valuations, bumper earnings and generous shareholder returns. While most investors see the latest DeepSeek development as a short-term setback, the latest declines show the rebound would not be linear.

“DeepSeek’s new model could stoke concerns about a slowdown in semiconductor demand in the near term,” Eugene Asset Management chief investment officer Ha SeokKeun said. Still, new models from the likes of Meta Platforms Inc and OpenAI “will have a greater impact on the industry’s fundamentals by boosting actual AI usage and semiconductor demand.”

Local retail traders drove a feverish rally in Samsung and SK Hynix earlier this year before abruptly reversing course on a severe bout of AI skepticism. They have been rapidly exiting leveraged exchange-traded funds tied to the chipmakers, and have sold about US$10 billion worth of the two stocks this month alone.

Daily swings being less dictated by the whims of retail investors has tempted the return of some foreign funds, which have been large sellers year to date.

“We are definitely more positive on [South] Korean memory chipmakers than anything else in semiconductors,” said Isaac Thong, senior investment director and manager of the Aberdeen Asian Income Fund in Singapore. Based on a blend of price-to-book and price-to-earnings valuations, “these stocks look cheap, especially compared to global peers,” he added.

Samsung trades at 2.7 times current book value and SK Hynix at five times, compared with 11 times for the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index. The South Korean memory stocks are trading at about four times forward estimated earnings, versus 19 times for the gauge of global chipmakers.

However, the two South Korean memory stocks remain more than 25 percent below their all-time highs, with investors still spooked by wild swings on daily news and position adjustments.

“These names are going to be volatile. For most investors, there are ways to get the same returns with a lot less volatility,” Tuttle Capital Management chief executive officer Matthew Tuttle said.

Despite the decrease in leverage and measures implemented by regulators to restore calm, daily moves of 5 percent or more are still common for Samsung and SK Hynix. Given the strong fundamentals, foreign investors might return when there is a significant decrease in volatility, Fibonacci Asset Management Global chief executive officer Jung In Yun said.

data.title: Pig paradise
data.description: Mediterranean black pigs roam among tourists at a beach on Atokos island on Thursday. Atokos, a private island located off the coast of western Greece, has gained popularity on social media for its population of free-roaming Mediterranean black pigs. The uninhabited island has become a popular stop for boats and visitors, who come to swim in its waters and see the pigs roaming freely around the island.

data.title: Hedge fund UG courts Taiwan to tap AI wealth
data.description:
MILLIONAIRES’ MARKET: Banks and asset managers are racing to offer more private-market products to high-net-worth clients in Taiwan as their fortunes swell

UG Investment Advisers, a hedge fund overseeing US$3.7 billion, is targeting Taiwan’s wealthy as a new source of capital, betting on a surge in private fortunes fueled by the nation’s artificial intelligence (AI) boom.

The Singapore-headquartered firm signed a deal with Taiwan’s E.Sun Commercial Bank Ltd (玉山銀行) last month to distribute one of its long-short equity funds, its first tie-up with a local lender.

The move marks a homecoming of sorts for the hedge fund, which has roots in Taipei, but has largely relied on offshore investors such as Asian and European family offices for almost three decades.

“AI is rapidly creating new wealth in Taiwan, while the regulatory environment is becoming more favorable as the government pushes to develop the island into a financial hub,” UG Investment chief operating officer Brandy Chen said in an interview. “The stars are aligned for us to enter the onshore market.”

Banks and asset managers in Taiwan are racing to offer more private-market products to high-net-worth clients as their fortunes swell. The wealth boom is being fueled by the nation’s buoyant economy and stock market, underpinned by local chipmakers and sprawling supply-chain companies.

Taiwanese banks have made distribution deals with other global investment firms. Cathay United Bank Co (國泰世華銀行) said last month it was partnering with Carlyle Group Inc to sell private equity offerings to wealthy individuals in the nation’s dedicated wealth zone. CTBC Bank Co (中信銀行) teamed up with European private equity firm Ardian to offer funds investing in the secondaries market.

Offshore private equity, private credit and hedge funds must be distributed to Taiwanese individual investors through licensed banks or asset managers. Each fund is capped at 99 investors with at least NT$30 million (US$953,000) in assets, a limit the Financial Supervisory Commission (FSC) has pledged to ease as demand for alternative investments grows.

The outstanding balance of private funds sold to high-net-worth clients totals NT$7.38 billion, the FSC said earlier this year. That accounts for just 0.32 percent of the total assets under management for high-net-worth clients, a relatively small share.

Taiwan has more millionaires as a percentage of the adult population than anywhere else in Asia, with the exception of Hong Kong and Australia, according to this year’s UBS Global Wealth Report.

“The wealth creation is opening up onshore opportunities, while the rise of family offices reflects the new fortunes being minted by Taiwan’s AI supply chain,” Chen said.

UG Investment runs a 43-person team of fund managers, analysts and quants across Singapore, Shanghai and Taipei that pursue long-term, fundamental-driven strategies, she said.

UG’s largest fund, which it plans to offer in Taiwan, manages more than US$2 billion and focuses on technology stocks across the US and Asia, Chen said.

It has gained 14.2 percent in the first seven months of the year, despite a 2.5 percent drop in July amid a global tech selloff.

The fund has delivered an annualized return of 15.4 percent since inception in 2007, she said.

“Equity long-short hedge fund products are still relatively rare in Taiwan,” Chen said.

Most alternative offerings currently concentrate in private credit, private equity and infrastructure.

“We want to get ahead of the market,” she said.
